Introduction
The Preventive Cardiovascular Nurses Association (PCNA) 
recognizes that implementing guidelines-based treatment for 
patients with, or at risk for, Heart Failure (HF) can slow the 
progression of HF, lead to improved patient outcomes, and 
quality of life.
HF by the Numbers 
Of all American adults 40 and older, one in five will develop 
HF in their lifetime. Today, more than 6 million Americans 
live with HF; the number is predicted to continue to rise to an 
estimated 8 million Americans by 2030. There are racial and 
ethnic disparities in HF morbidity and mortality outcomes 
with non-Hispanic Black patients having the highest death rate 
per capita. These disparities warrant further studies and health 
policy changes to address inequity.

Common Causes of HF
•	 Ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction (MI)
•	 Hypertension
•	 Valvular heart disease (VHD)
Other/Non-ischemic Causes of HF
•	 Familial or genetic cardiomyopathies
•	 Amyloidosis and other infiltrative cardiac diseases
•	 Cardiotoxicity with cancer or other treatments, or substance 
abuse such as alcohol, cocaine, or methamphetamine
•	 Tachycardia or right ventricular (RV) pacing
•	 Peripartum or stress-induced cardiomyopathies
•	 Myocarditis
•	 Autoimmune causes, sarcoidosis
•	 Iron overload, including hemochromatosis
•	 Thyroid disease and other endocrine, metabolic, and 
nutritional causes

Examination

Lifestyle Management and Self Care
Sodium restriction:
• For Stage C HF, avoiding excessive sodium intake is
reasonable to reduce congestive symptoms.
• The AHA currently recommends a reduction of sodium
intake to <2300 mg/d of daily sodium for general
cardiovascular health.
Fluid restriction:
• Fluid restriction (1.5 to 2 L/d) may be prescribed in acute or
advanced HF and hyponatremia.
Smoking and alcohol use:
• Smoking cessation should be strongly encouraged.
• Counsel patients to limit alcohol use.
o ≤2 drinks per day for men and ≤1 drink per day for women.
Exercise and Cardiac Rehabilitation
• Exercise training (or regular physical activity) is
recommended to improve functional status exercise
performance and quality of life (QOL).
• Cardiac rehabilitation can be useful in clinically stable
patients with HF to improve functional capacity, exercise
duration, health-related QOL, and mortality.
• Consider a referral to cardiac rehabilitation following an
admission for acute HF.
• Cardiac rehabilitation may be considered for those with
HFpEF, however, insurance coverage is unlikely at this time.

10
Multidisciplinary Care
• Care by a multidisciplinary team is recommended to
facilitate Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT),
address barriers to self-care, reduce risk of
re-hospitalization, and improve survival.
• Specific education and support to facilitate HF self-care
including: how to take medications, restrict sodium
intake, stay physically active, get vaccines, self-monitor for
signs and symptoms of worsening HF, and what to do in
response to symptoms.
• Screen for depression, social isolation, frailty, and low
health literacy as risk factors for poor self-care.
• Vaccinate against respiratory illnesses.

HF Pharmacotherapies and Management  
of Comorbid Conditions
Key Points:
•	 GDMT for HFrEF includes a beta blocker, ACEi/ARB/ARNi, 
MRA, and SGLT2i. These four medication classes should be 
initiated and optimized to maximally-tolerated dose.
•	 Only guideline-recommended beta 
blockers (i.e., carvedilol, metoprolol 
succinate, or bisoprolol) should be used 
in patients with HFrEF.
•	 For persistently symptomatic Black patients, in addition 
to above therapies, consider hydralazine and isosorbide 
dinitrate.
•	 Despite maximally-tolerated beta blocker, if resting HR is 
≥70 bpm in sinus rhythm, ivabradine may be considered.
•	 Adjustment of therapies should be considered every 2 weeks 
to achieve GDMT within 3-6 months of initial diagnosis.
•	 Continue GDMT in HFrEF and HFimpEF.
•	 Consider SGLT2i in HFpEF and HFmrEF.
•	 ARNi recommended in HFpEF.
Recommended therapies for those with HF and comorbidities
•	 Hypertension: optimal treatment of BP per guidelines
•	 Diabetes: SGLT2i for management of hyperglycemia
•	 Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation; consider CRT, ablation
•	 Iron deficiency: IV iron replacement
•	 Obstructive sleep apnea: CPAP
•	 Cancer therapy related cardiomyopathy: ARB, ACEi, and 
beta blockers

Drug Class: ACEi, ARB, or ARNi
Reduces morbidity and mortality in HF. Choose one from this class, unless 
contraindicated. Renal function and potassium should be checked within 
1-2 weeks of initiation or dose up-titration of ACEi/ARB/ARNi.
Caution using ACEi, ARB or ARNi:
•	 Renal insufficiency
•	 Volume depleted
•	 Pregnant or plan to become pregnant
•	 Do not use ARNi with a history of angioedema
•	 Do not use ARNi within 36 hours of the last dose of an ACEi

Drug Class: Beta Blockers
Recommended to treat patients with current, or prior, symptoms of HFrEF 
to reduce morbidity and mortality. Choose one of the four, approved for 
HF, unless contraindicated.
Beta blockers should be started as soon as LV dysfunction is 
diagnosed, at low doses; gradually increased as tolerated.
Caution using beta blocker:
• Edema/fluid retention
• High degree AV block
• Asthma or bronchoconstriction (carvedilol)
Drug Class: Mineralcorticoid Receptor Antagonist (MRA)
Recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality in patients with HFrEF 
and NYHA class II to IV symptoms.
• MRA use increases the risk of hyperkalemia or renal
insufficiency when serum creatinine is greater than 2.5 
mg/dL in men, or greater than 2.0 mg/dL in women (or
estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2),
and/or potassium greater than 5.0 mEq/L.
• A basic metabolic panel (BMP) is recommended within one
week of initiating or titrating MRA to monitor potassium,
renal function, and diuretic dosing.
• The incidence of gynecomastia is higher with spironolactone
than eplerenone.

Drug Class: SGLT2-Inhibitor (SGLT2i)
Reduces the risk of cardiovascular (CV) death and hospitalization for HF.
•	 Not approved for use in patients with type 1 diabetes due 
to increased risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
•	 Temporary discontinuation 3 days before scheduled surgery 
is recommended to avoid potential risk for ketoacidosis.
•	 Assess patients who present with signs and symptoms of 
metabolic acidosis for ketoacidosis, regardless of blood 
glucose level.
•	 May contribute to volume depletion. Consider altering 
diuretic dose, if applicable.
•	 Increases risk of mycotic genital infections.
Drug Class: If Channel Inhibitor
Reduces the risk of hospitalization for worsening HF in adult patients with 
stable, symptomatic chronic HF with LVEF ≤35%, who are in sinus rhythm 
with resting HR ≥70 beats-per-minute, and either are on maximally-
tolerated beta blockers or if beta blocker use is contraindicated.
•	 In those who have a history of conduction defects, or 
adults in whom bradycardia could lead to hemodynamic 
compromise, decrease initial dose to 2.5 mg PO BID; may 
increase dose based on heart rate.
•	 Contraindicated in acute decompensated HF, BP < 90/50 
mmHg, pretreatment HR < 60 bpm, severe hepatic 
impairment, pacemaker dependence, sick sinus syndrome, 
SA block, or 3rd degree heart block, unless a functioning 
demand pacemaker is in use.

Drug Class: Hydralazine/Isosorbide
Reduces morbidity or mortality in patients with current or prior 
symptomatic HFrEF who cannot be given an ACEi or ARB because of drug 
intolerance, hypotension, or renal insufficiency, unless contraindicated.
• In Black patients, the addition of hydralazine and
isosorbide dinitrate to standard therapy improves survival
and decreases hospitalization.
Drug Class: Digoxin
Can be beneficial in patients with HFrEF, unless contraindicated, to 
decrease hospitalizations for HF.
• Clinicians may consider adding digoxin in patients with
persistent symptoms of HFrEF during GDMT.
• Patients should not be given digoxin if they have significant 
sinus or atrioventricular block, unless the block has been
addressed with a permanent pacemaker.
• Use cautiously in patients taking other drugs that can
depress sinus or atrioventricular nodal function, or affect 
digoxin levels.

Drug Class: Soluble Guanylate Cyclase Stimulator
In selected high-risk patients with HFrEF and recent worsening of HF 
already on GDMT, an oral soluble guanylate cylase stimulator (vericiguat) 
may be considered to reduce HF hospitalization and CV death.
•	 Monitor patients for symptomatic hypotension or syncope.
Drug Class: Diuretics
Recommended for all patients who have evidence of, and to most 
patients with a prior history of, fluid retention. Diuretics should generally 
be combined with an ACEi, beta blocker, and MRA.
•	 The principal adverse effects of diuretics include electrolyte 
and fluid depletion, as well as hypotension and azotemia 
(elevated blood nitrogen).
•	 Diuretics can cause the depletion of potassium and magnesium, 
which can predispose patients to serious cardiac arrhythmias.
•	 The risk of electrolyte depletion is markedly enhanced 
when two diuretics are used in combination.
•	 Check BUN/Cr, serum CO2, and electrolytes frequently 
early in treatment, then periodically.

Therapeutic Management Beyond Pharmacotherapies
Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT): 
• LV systolic dysfunction and dyssynchronous ventricular
activation provides simultaneous electrical activation of the
LV and right ventricle (RV) via stimulation of the LV and
RV (biventricular pacing), or LV alone.
Implantable Cardio-Defibrillator (ICD):
• Secondary prevention sudden cardiac death (SCD) with
prior sustained ventricular arrhythmia.
o Including valvular, ischemic, hypertrophic, dilated or
infiltrative cardiomyopathy (CM).
• Primary prevention of SCD in patients who are at risk of
life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
o Prior MI at least 40 days ago, and LVEF <35%.
o CM, NYHA II or III, and LVEF <35%.
ICD/CRT for volume management:
• Indirect measures of volume accumulation/increased
filling pressures measurement of intrathoracic impedance 
or by multisensory algorithm; examples: OptiVol system,
MultiSENSE system.
Implanted remote pulmonary artery (PA) pressure 
monitoring system:
• Implantable miniature sensor system which monitors PA 
systolic pressure, PA diastolic pressure, mean PA pressure,
and HR.
• Values are monitored remotely and can aid in early
detection of worsening HF, and treatment decision-making.
• Indicated for NYHA III; history of HF hospitalization or
elevated NP levels, once GDMT is optimized.

21
Coronary Revascularization:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery 
bypass graft surgery (CABG); indications specific to HF:
•	 PCI or CABG in HFpEF and HFrEF on GDMT with angina 
and suitable coronary anatomy, especially for a left main 
stenosis (>50%) or left main equivalent disease.
•	 CABG in mild- to moderate-LV systolic dysfunction (EF 
35% to 50%) and significant (≥70% diameter stenosis) 
multivessel CAD, or proximal left anterior descending 
coronary artery stenosis when viable myocardium is 
present in the region of intended revascularization.
•	 CABG or medical therapy is reasonable to improve 
morbidity and cardiovascular mortality for patients with 
severe LV dysfunction (EF <35%), HF, and significant CAD.
•	 CABG may be considered with the intent of improving 
survival in patients with ischemic heart disease with severe 
LV systolic dysfunction (EF <35%) and operable coronary 
anatomy, whether or not viable myocardium is present.
Valvular Heart Disease (VHD)
VHD is a significant cause of HF. GDMT applies to all 
patients with HFrEF, irrespective of the presence of VHD. 
Significant VHD warrants evaluation and management by a 
multidisciplinary VHD specialty team, and in accordance with 
accepted clinical practice guidelines to prevent worsening HF 
and adverse clinical outcomes. 
•	 With chronic severe secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) 
and HFrEF, optimization of GDMT is recommended 
before any intervention for secondary MR related to LV 
dysfunction. 
•	 In symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS), transcatheter 
and surgical aortic valve repair can improve survival, 
symptoms, and LV function.

22
• Management of tricuspid regurgitation should focus on
underlying causes, such as pulmonary hypertension, RV
failure, and HFrEF.
Cardiac Amyloidosis
Cardiac amyloidosis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy with 
extracellular myocardial protein deposition, most commonly 
monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains amyloid cardiomyopathy 
(AL-CM), or transthyretin amyloidosis cardiomyopathy (ATTR-
CM). Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) can be caused by gene 
variation or wild-type transthyretin. LV thickening along with 
fatigue, dyspnea, or edema are signs and symptoms of cardiac 
amyloidosis.
• When there is a suspicion for cardiac amyloidosis, screen for
serum and urine monoclonal light chains with serum and urine 
immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chains.
• If there is a high suspicion for cardiac amyloidosis without
evidence of serum or urine monoclonal light chains, bone
scintigraphy is recommended to confirm the presence of
transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.
• When diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis
is made, genetic testing with transthyretin (TTR) gene
sequencing is recommended to differentiate hereditary
variant from wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.
• Treatment with transthyretin tetramer stabilizer therapy
(tafamidis) is indicated to reduce cardiac morbidity and
mortality in those with wild-type or variant transthyretin
cardiac amyloidosis and NYHA class I to III HF symptoms.
• Anticoagulation is reasonable in those with cardiac
amyloidosis and atrial fibrillation (AF) to reduce the risk of 
stroke regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score.

Referral to a HF specialist should be considered in patients needing

heart rate, and progressive intolerance to GDMT needing down-titration.

24
Palliative and End-of-Life Care
Advances in HF care delay the progression of disease but rarely 
lead to a cure, such that palliative care needs of the patient 
must be considered. A formal palliative care consultation may 
be helpful for those with refractory symptoms, major medical 
decisions, multimorbidity, frailty, or cognitive impairment. 
These principles guide clinicians in an end-of-life plan:
•	 Reduce pain and manage symptoms while integrating 
psychological and spiritual care.
•	 Good HF management is cornerstone of symptom 
palliation.
•	 Palliative care consultation and complementary approaches 
to care may further ameliorate refractory HF symptoms and 
improve patient satisfaction and quality of life.
•	 Patients with HF often face major treatment decisions over 
time and should be provided with support when thinking 
through the benefits and burdens of each treatment option.
•	 Proactive shared decision-making discussions simplify 
difficult decisions in the future.
•	 The clinical trajectory is required to calibrate expectations 
and guide timely decisions, but prognostic uncertainty 
is inevitable and should be included in discussions with 
patients and caregivers.
•	 The transition from “do everything” to “comfort only/
